key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can introduce hidden data leakage into protein–protein interaction (PPI) inference workflows, producing artificially inflated performance metrics; rigorous evaluation controls are needed to detect and prevent this artifact.
problem_solved: Exposes and characterizes how pLM-derived features can leak information across training and test sets in PPI prediction, leading to misleading model assessment and overoptimistic claims.
method: Empirical comparisons of PPI models trained with and without pLM-derived embeddings to quantify performance inflation.
Diagnostic analyses to trace leakage sources (e.g., shared pretraining data, embedding similarity, homologous sequences) using controlled splits and ablation studies.
Recommendations of mitigation and evaluation practices (e.g., homology-aware splits, embedding deconfounding, stricter benchmarking) to obtain honest performance estimates.
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners in computational biology that off-the-shelf pretrained embeddings can distort evaluation, motivating stricter dataset design and reproducible benchmarking so PPI models reflect real generalization.
visual_elements: Flow diagram showing how pretraining data and embeddings can propagate into training/test sets and create leakage paths.
Bar chart comparing reported (inflated) vs. corrected PPI performance scores with and without pLM embeddings or with proper controls.
Schematic illustrating dataset splitting strategies (random split vs. homology-aware split) and their effect on leakage.
Icon cluster: warning/shield symbol, protein chain illustrations, and an embedding/model icon to signal caution with pretrained models.
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
